source_refs.note: Book p. 22: 2.1.1 Definition (function, domain, range, codomain; sets of real numbers).
Book p. 23: the pink Note box (co-domain vs range) printed at the top of the page belongs to 2.1.1. Tables, Teaching notes, Key points and Common mistake are ours.

blocks.text: A function \(f\) from a set \(X\) to a set \(Y\) is a rule or a correspondence that assigns to each element \(x\) in \(X\) a unique element \(y\) in \(Y\). The set \(X\) is called the domain of \(f\).
The set of corresponding elements \(y\) in \(Y\) is called the range of \(f\). The codomain of a function is the set \(Y\) in which the function's output values (the range) lie.
Unless stated otherwise, we shall assume from now on that the sets \(X\) and \(Y\) consist of real numbers.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Co-domain is the set of all possible outputs, but the range is the actual set of outputs produced by the function on the given domain. So the range is always a subset of the co-domain.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A function from \(X\) to \(Y\) is written \(f : X \to Y\) (read "\(f\) from \(X\) to \(Y\)"). Think of three sets:
Domain \(X\): all the inputs we are allowed to use.
Co-domain \(Y\): the set where the outputs are allowed to land (it is chosen when the function is defined).
Range: the outputs that actually occur. It is found by applying \(f\) to every element of the domain.
So always: range \(\subseteq\) co-domain.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read the table above. Each element of the domain \(X = \{1, 2, 3\}\) has exactly one output, so \(f\) is a function from \(X\) to \(Y\).
Domain \(= \{1, 2, 3\}\)
Co-domain \(= Y = \{1, 4, 9, 16\}\)
Range \(= \{1, 4, 9\}\)
The element \(16\) is in the co-domain but no input gives it, so it is not in the range. This is exactly the difference the Note describes.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When asked "is this a function?", check the two conditions on the domain one by one: (1) every input has an output, (2) no input has two outputs. Give the exact input that fails, e.g. "not a function, because \(1\) has two images \(a\) and \(b\)".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(f : X \to Y\) assigns to every \(x \in X\) a unique \(y \in Y\).
2. Domain = set of inputs \(X\).
3. Co-domain = set \(Y\) where outputs may lie.
4. Range = set of outputs actually produced; range \(\subseteq\) co-domain.
5. In this book, \(X\) and \(Y\) are sets of real numbers unless stated otherwise.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the co-domain when the range is asked. The range contains only the outputs that really occur.
2. Thinking every element of \(Y\) must be used. Only every element of \(X\) must be used; elements of \(Y\) may be left out.
3. Calling a rule a function when some element of the domain has no output.
